moe: add DeepEP V2 ElasticBuffer probe and opt-in buffer path
…
1d6b522
DeepEP V2 (
deepseek-ai/DeepEP#605
, merged 2026-04-29) introduces
`ElasticBuffer` alongside the legacy `Buffer`. Both classes are
exported from `deep_ep.__init__`, so SGLang's existing V1 code path
continues to work unchanged on a V2 install.

This patch adds a second import probe (`have_deepep_v2`) next to the
existing `use_deepep` flag, then lets users opt in to the V2
`ElasticBuffer` ctor behind `SGLANG_DEEPEP_USE_V2=1`. The V1 path is
byte-identical when the env var is unset, so this is a backwards-
compatible addition.

V2 collapses the V1 NVL/RDMA byte-pool ctor into a single MoE-shape
ctor and derives the internal buffer size from `num_max_tokens_per_rank`,
`hidden`, and `num_topk`. `num_allocated_qps=0` asks V2 to auto-size
and auto-cap the Queue-Pair budget on AWS EFA (the 128-slot GIN ring
ceiling; see `_is_efa_fabric` in `deep_ep/buffers/elastic.py`).

Why:
- Removes the need for users to monkeypatch `deep_ep.Buffer` to reach
  V2 semantics, and mirrors the probe shape already used in
  NVIDIA/Megatron-LM's `fused_a2a.py` (`HAVE_DEEP_EP_V2`). Opt-in
  env-var gate keeps the change infra-bump-shaped, not a default
  switch flip.
- vLLM is landing a parallel native-V2 path in
vllm-project/vllm#41183
(16 commits, active review). SGLang users
  running mixed-framework MoE stacks benefit from having V2 reachable
  in SGLang without a runtime monkeypatch.

V2 parity rules baked in:
- `num_max_tokens_per_rank` sourced from
  `envs.SGLANG_DEEPEP_NUM_MAX_DISPATCH_TOKENS_PER_RANK` when the
  caller did not pin it (matches the V1 low-latency path).
- `num_topk=0` at ctor time: DeepEP V2 accepts this and derives a
  conservative group-size-based hint, so we don't need to know the
  router topk at buffer construction.
- `clean_buffer()` skips the legacy `clean_low_latency_buffer` call
  when the underlying buffer is an ElasticBuffer (no equivalent on
  V2, per `deep_ep/buffers/elastic.py`).

NVSHMEM aliases nvshmemi_ibgda_device_state_t to the _v2 struct since 3.5,

title: Fix mega_mhc split barriers under CUDA graph replay
body:
A CUDA graph kernel node keeps the same `%gridid` on every replay. The `mega_mhc` split barriers tag executions with `%gridid`, so after a replay a barrier line still holds `encode_state(grid_idx, kNumSplits)` — exactly what the next replay waits for. A Mix or Norm waiter whose m-block init CTA has not started yet proceeds at once and reads the previous replay's split partials (the graph-pool scratch is the same memory). `wait_init` only protects producers.

This tags each execution with an epoch instead of `%gridid`. The epoch and an exit count live in the unused tail of the first barrier line, so the host-side barrier buffer and the compiled extension are unchanged (JIT headers only). Every CTA reads the epoch after `cudaGridDependencySynchronize()`; the last CTA to retire resets the exit count and advances the epoch.

The MegaMoE combine readiness has the same stale-tag problem and is addressed separately in #451.

Validation on B200: one graph node is replayed while alternating two input sets, and every replay is compared bit for bit with eager results (fresh JIT cache per run). Measured on 66081d4, whose versions of these headers differ from `main` only by an added `#include`.

| case | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| 33 tokens, SMs contended by another stream | 185/200 wrong | 0/400 |
| 512 tokens, contended | 27/200 | 0/400 |
| 8192 tokens, contended | 3/200 | 0/400 |
| 512 tokens, idle GPU | 1/200 | 0/400 |

Eager calls, and graph replays preceded by an eager launch that rewrites the tag, were 0/200 before the fix as well.

How it works
The kernel fixes the order first. The B loader enumerates a stream in which a token block's L2 tasks sit
lag
units after its L1 tasks, in groups of
group
units; a unit is up to 8 consecutive m-blocks of one expert. The host picks
lag = clamp(round(0.45 × units), 8, 64)
and
group = 4
, with
units
estimated from the call's token bound and the buffer capacity, not the routed count.
It also differs from
#383
numerically: one scale per 64 or 128 contiguous K elements of the intermediate activation (
l2_act_sf_gran_k
, a buffer parameter) where
#383
always writes one per 64, and the raw scale where
#383
's SM90 kernel rounds it to the next power of two. Both are inside the shared test's tolerance against the same reference.
Why the order and not the pool size, and the lag ladder
The split path materialises every rank's L1 output before L2 starts, so its pool is sized for all tokens of all ranks and the GEMMs never overlap. Fusing them buys the overlap and does not fix the pool, because nothing bounds how far L2 trails L1. Worse, L2's NVLink combine scatter starts while the dispatch pull is still running on the same per-rank egress. A ladder that pins the ring at 356 blocks and varies only the lag still leaves the short-lag calls the slow ones, so what costs is the order and not the pool size.
Event traces on an instrumented build of this kernel (8×H100, 8192 tokens/rank) put the end of the dispatch pull at 2671 µs from kernel start when the lag is 8 units and at 1102 µs when it is 40 — 2541 µs against 1044 µs measured from each run's own head barrier, which completes at 130 µs and at 58 µs. At the lag this picks, 55 % of the L1 tiles are done when the pull ends.
Ring sizing, recycling, and why that granularity
Fixing the order makes the ring size arithmetic: at most
8 × (lag + group)
blocks of L1 output are live, so the pool becomes a ring of
8 × (lag + group) + 4
slots, asserted against that live set on the host. L1 epilogues wait on
l2_empty
before overwriting a slot's previous generation, and dispatch warps publish any pending arrival before blocking, so no wait can point at unpublished work.
kSm90FusedLagRingMargin
is the
+ 4
. Recycling reuses the
l1/l2_full
counters and adds the matching
empty
counters plus launch-parity banks for the flags that would otherwise need all-rank head and exit barriers. A ring clamped to the full pool never wraps and is exempt from the host assertion. Consumers replay the tile table the B loader publishes — payload first, then an acquire-loaded tag — and the L2 tail after the last L1 task is handed out by an atomic ticket. Calls whose worst-case pool already fits, and buffers below the lag threshold, keep a single-wave order instead.
Also in the diff: arrival publishes batched up to 16 rows, on calls above a token threshold whose ring covers the batch; an early combine in which math warps reduce tokens whose selected experts have all published while the all-rank barrier is still pending; a BLOCK_M=64, 256-wide split-N tile with a sliced combine queue for decode-sized calls;
num_tokens_bound
; and an XOR bank swizzle on the L2 epilogue staging. The early combine stages whole rows in the pre-barrier shared memory where they fit and in chunks otherwise, and falls back from 2 chunks to 4 when 2 do not fit — which is what keeps 7168 hidden working at decode sizes, where the tile leaves that region smallest.
The scale width defaults to 128 when
hidden % 512 == 0
and
2 × intermediate_hidden % 512 == 0
(the condition for the 256-wide decode tile) and to 64 otherwise. 128 is the grouping the non-fused DeepEP + grouped-GEMM path uses for this activation; it halves the act-SF pool and lets each 128-K step of L2's mainloop take one scale group and one rescale instead of two.
#360
reports an end-to-end accuracy issue it suspects came from quantising this same activation per-64 where the rest of the stack does per-128.
The scale itself is
sf = max(amax, 1e-10) / 448
, the raw scale, which is also what the shared test's reference computes (with a 1e-4 floor on amax instead of 1e-10) and what the sgl-project SM90 kernel this data path comes from uses. The fused arm keeps the full FP8 range, the split one keeps an exactly representable scale.

It must be identical on every rank and cover every rank's own count, e.g. the max over ranks of the local batch. Each rank rejects a bound below its own count or above the buffer's capacity, but nothing compares the ranks, and a bound below a peer's count hangs: this rank's pool is then sized for fewer rows than will arrive, so the ring reuses a slot inside one wave.

What a per-rank token count changes, and what it does not
The rules that key on a per-rank token count fall back to this rank's own count when the bound is omitted, so ranks with different local batches can pick different orders. Nothing cross-rank rides on that: the ring capacity is the buffer's, and the call's lag comes from the bound -- the capacity when none is given -- clamped to the buffer's, so both hold the same value on every rank.
One rule keys on the token count in a way worth spelling out.
block_m
is chosen from this rank's token count (
num_tokens * num_ranks * num_topk / num_experts >= 64
flips it 64 -> 128),
block_m
sets
num_stages
through the per-stage smem cost, and early combine turns on only when
hidden / block_k
and
intermediate_hidden / block_k
both exceed
num_stages
. So it is a function of the shapes only where the shape leaves margin, and passing
num_tokens_bound
does not make it uniform -- the tile choice reads the raw count. On the shapes here the margin is wide: 4096/2048 gives 16 k-blocks and 7168/3072 gives 24, against 3 stages at both M=2048 and M=8192, and the mode never flips. I had to take
intermediate_hidden
down to 640, which no shipped config uses, before the flip appeared -- 287 tokens gives 7 stages and mode 0, 288 gives 4 stages and mode 1. What does move per rank on production shapes is
block_m
,
block_n
and
num_stages
, and since those are JIT template arguments like the mode itself, ranks with different local batches compile and launch different instantiations of the same kernel. They still meet at the same pre-combine rendezvous: same signal word, same phase and sign rule, same expected arrival count, one signal per rank either way. If the modes ever did disagree the cost would be throughput, not liveness -- a rank on the early-combine path only early-combines tokens whose experts all live on ranks that took the same path, and the rest fall through to the ordinary combine after the barrier. One gap worth noting on its own: the early-combine copy of the barrier keeps the 60 s deadline on the cross-rank signal wait but not on its two grid syncs, which the shared
grid_sync

Add a fused SM90 FP8 MegaMoE with a lag-ordered ring schedule
…
cbd08d9
The Hopper MegaMoE runs its two linears as two kernels, so the whole linear-1 activation is written
to the symmetric buffer before linear 2 reads any of it, the two GEMMs cannot overlap, and the pool
grows with the token bound rather than with what the GEMMs have in flight. This adds a single-kernel
path next to it: one task stream in which a per-CTA tile table keeps linear 2 a bounded number of
tiles behind linear 1, with the linear-1 activation pool sized as a ring around that lag, so it only
holds the rows in flight. At the benchmark's 8192-token bound the symmetric buffer goes from 3023 to
700 MiB on 4096/2048/256/top-6 and from 5083 to 1113 MiB on 7168/3072/384/top-6.

The path is additive and opt-in: `fused=True` on the buffer size query allocates the ring buffer and
the buffer type then selects the kernel at launch, so the two-kernel path, its heuristics and its
launcher are untouched and its two Python entry points only gain keyword arguments whose defaults
dispatch exactly as they do today. The query also returns the ring capacity and the lag encoding,
and both travel back to the kernel on every launch together with the K granularity of the
intermediate activation scales (per-128 K where the 256-wide decode tile fits, per-64 K otherwise).
The default layout keeps the full pool below 1024 tokens per rank and rings above it; a caller can
still ask for a ring sized for a given expert wave, or for an automatically chosen one. Decode-sized
calls also take the programmatic dependent launch attribute, since their instantiation carries
griddepcontrol wait/trigger.

Issue body actions
Description
On SM90 GPUs, tf32_hc_prenorm_gemm can produce incorrect and non-deterministic GEMM outputs when processing multiple K blocks.
Repeated calls with identical inputs can return different results.
Root cause
The kernel uses asynchronous WGMMA instructions with register-source A operands. Previously, the next iteration loaded its A fragment
before waiting for the preceding iteration's WGMMA to complete. This could overwrite A registers while they were still being read by
the in-flight WGMMA.
Fix
Proposed fix:
#448
The fix moves
warpgroup_wait<0>()
immediately after
warpgroup_commit_batch()
, ensuring that each iteration's WGMMA completes
before its A registers are reused.
The PR also adds a regression test covering split-K, PDL enabled/disabled, and default/side streams. It checks outputs against FP32
references and verifies repeatability across identical launches.
Validation
With the fix applied, both the existing hyperconnection tests and all 24 configurations of the new regression test passed on an SM90
GPU.
TODO
fix will introduce some performance regression which suppose to be mitigated in upcoming PRs。

#448
's gain on the 16-split shapes. So it is not clearly better overall. The patch is on

From 29e4a0e3d029d2ac54587d4adaec71dbab09c0e9 Mon Sep 17 00:00:00 2001
From: Daoyuan Li <94409450+DaoyuanLi2816@users.noreply.github.com>
Date: Wed, 8 Jul 2026 22:34:33 -0700
Subject: [PATCH] Add Sequential Temperature Scaling for confidence-head
 calibration

The DSpark paper (Section 3.2.1) calibrates the confidence head with
Sequential Temperature Scaling (STS): for each block position, left to
right, a 1D grid search picks the temperature that minimizes the ECE of
the cumulative prefix-survival probability, keeping earlier positions
fixed. The evaluator already measures exactly that quantity
(per-position cumulative-product ECE / AUROC / reliability diagrams),
but the calibration itself was missing, and raw confidence scores are
noticeably overconfident.

This adds the full offline STS workflow:

- eval.py --confidence-dump-dir writes per-proposal confidence records
  ((logits, prefix-accept labels) per dataset) for offline fitting.
- scripts/fit_confidence_calibration.py fits per-position temperatures
  from dumped records via the paper's left-to-right grid search and
  reports cumulative ECE before/after at each position.
- eval.py --confidence-calibration-path applies the fitted temperatures
  to the confidence logits during evaluation, so both the reported
  calibration metrics and the --confidence-threshold early stop consume
  calibrated probabilities.

With deepseek-ai/dspark_qwen3_4b_block7 on Qwen/Qwen3-4B, fitting on
gsm8k and evaluating held-out (temperature 1.0, threshold 0, identical
seeds so generation is unchanged): alpaca ece_mean 0.0893 -> 0.0315 and
mt-bench 0.0697 -> 0.0224, with AUROC unchanged (0.8530 -> 0.8516 and
0.8693 -> 0.8686), confirming the calibration is order-preserving.
Fitted temperatures are all > 1, matching the paper's overconfidence
observation.

+++ b/scripts/fit_confidence_calibration.py
@@ -0,0 +1,258 @@
+"""Fit Sequential Temperature Scaling (STS) for the DSpark confidence head.
+
+Implements the post-hoc calibration described in the DSpark paper
+(Section 3.2.1): for each block position k (left to right), a 1D grid
+search selects a temperature scalar that minimizes the Expected
+Calibration Error (ECE) of the cumulative prefix-survival probability
+
+    a_k = prod_{i <= k} sigmoid(logit_i / T_i),
+
+keeping the already-fitted temperatures of all preceding positions
+fixed. Temperature scaling is order-preserving, so it rectifies the
+absolute probability magnitudes without changing the confidence head's
+token ranking.
+
+Input records are produced by evaluation runs with
+``eval.py --confidence-dump-dir <dir>`` (run them with
+``--confidence-threshold 0`` and without ``--confidence-calibration-path``
+so the dumped logits are uncalibrated and blocks are untruncated). Fit on
+a held-out split, then pass the resulting JSON to
+``eval.py --confidence-calibration-path``.
+
+Example:
+    python scripts/fit_confidence_calibration.py \
+        --records confidence_records/gsm8k/confidence_records.jsonl \
+        --output confidence_calibration.json
+"""
+
+from __future__ import annotations
+
+import argparse
+import json
+import math
+from pathlib import Path
+
+import torch
+
+
+EPS_PROB = 1e-8
+
+
+def parse_args() -> argparse.Namespace:
+    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(
+        description=(
+            "Fit per-position confidence temperatures (Sequential "
+            "Temperature Scaling) from dumped confidence records."
+        ),
+    )
+    parser.add_argument(
+        "--records",
+        nargs="+",
+        required=True,
+        help="One or more confidence_records.jsonl files to fit on.",
+    )
+    parser.add_argument(
+        "--output",
+        required=True,
+        help="Output JSON path for the fitted calibration.",
+    )
+    parser.add_argument(
+        "--num-bins",
+        type=int,
+        default=20,
+        help="Equal-width ECE bins; matches the evaluator's coarse bins.",
+    )
+    parser.add_argument(
+        "--grid-min",
+        type=float,
+        default=0.05,
+        help="Smallest temperature in the search grid.",
+    )
+    parser.add_argument(
+        "--grid-max",
+        type=float,
+        default=20.0,
+        help="Largest temperature in the search grid.",
+    )
+    parser.add_argument(
+        "--grid-size",
+        type=int,
+        default=256,
+        help="Number of log-spaced grid points between grid-min and grid-max.",
+    )
+    return parser.parse_args()
+
+
+def load_records(paths: list[str]) -> tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]:
+    """Load ragged (logits, labels) rows into padded tensors plus a valid mask."""
+    logits_rows: list[list[float]] = []
+    label_rows: list[list[int]] = []
+    for path in paths:
+        with Path(path).open("r", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
+            for line_number, line in enumerate(handle, start=1):
+                line = line.strip()
+                if not line:
+                    continue
+                record = json.loads(line)
+                logits = [float(value) for value in record["logits"]]
+                labels = [int(value) for value in record["labels"]]
+                assert len(logits) == len(labels) and len(logits) > 0, (
+                    f"{path}:{line_number} has mismatched or empty "
+                    f"logits/labels ({len(logits)} vs {len(labels)})."
+                )
+                logits_rows.append(logits)
+                label_rows.append(labels)
+    assert logits_rows, f"No records found in: {', '.join(paths)}"
+
+    block_size = max(len(row) for row in logits_rows)
+    num_records = len(logits_rows)
+    logits = torch.zeros((num_records, block_size), dtype=torch.float64)
+    labels = torch.zeros((num_records, block_size), dtype=torch.float64)
+    valid = torch.zeros((num_records, block_size), dtype=torch.bool)
+    for row_idx, (logit_row, label_row) in enumerate(zip(logits_rows, label_rows)):
+        length = len(logit_row)
+        logits[row_idx, :length] = torch.tensor(logit_row, dtype=torch.float64)
+        labels[row_idx, :length] = torch.tensor(label_row, dtype=torch.float64)
+        valid[row_idx, :length] = True
+    return logits, labels, valid
+
+
+def expected_calibration_error(
+    probs: torch.Tensor,
+    targets: torch.Tensor,
+    *,
+    num_bins: int,
+) -> float:
+    """Equal-width-bin ECE; mirrors PerPositionConfidenceMetrics."""
+    probs = probs.clamp(EPS_PROB, 1.0 - EPS_PROB)
+    bin_idx = (probs * num_bins).long().clamp_(0, num_bins - 1)
+    ones = torch.ones_like(probs)
+    count = torch.zeros(num_bins, dtype=torch.float64).scatter_add_(0, bin_idx, ones)
+    pred = torch.zeros(num_bins, dtype=torch.float64).scatter_add_(0, bin_idx, probs)
+    target = torch.zeros(num_bins, dtype=torch.float64).scatter_add_(
+        0, bin_idx, targets
+    )
+    total = float(count.sum().item())
+    if total <= 0.0:
+        return float("nan")
+    denom = count.clamp_min(1e-12)
+    bin_err = (pred / denom - target / denom).abs()
+    return float((bin_err * count).sum().item() / total)
+
+
+def fit_sequential_temperatures(
+    *,
+    logits: torch.Tensor,
+    labels: torch.Tensor,
+    valid: torch.Tensor,
+    grid: torch.Tensor,
+    num_bins: int,
+) -> tuple[list[float], list[float], list[float]]:
+    block_size = logits.shape[1]
+    temperatures: list[float] = []
+    ece_before: list[float] = []
+    ece_after: list[float] = []
+    calibrated_cumprod = torch.ones(logits.shape[0], dtype=torch.float64)
+    raw_cumprod = torch.ones(logits.shape[0], dtype=torch.float64)
+
+    for position in range(block_size):
+        position_valid = valid[:, position]
+        num_valid = int(position_valid.sum().item())
+        if num_valid == 0:
+            temperatures.append(1.0)
+            ece_before.append(float("nan"))
+            ece_after.append(float("nan"))
+            continue
+
+        position_logits = logits[position_valid, position]
+        position_labels = labels[position_valid, position]
+        prefix = calibrated_cumprod[position_valid]
+
+        raw_probs = raw_cumprod[position_valid] * torch.sigmoid(position_logits)
+        ece_before.append(
+            expected_calibration_error(
+                raw_probs,
+                position_labels,
+                num_bins=num_bins,
+            )
+        )
+
+        best_temperature = 1.0
+        best_ece = float("inf")
+        for temperature in grid.tolist():
+            probs = prefix * torch.sigmoid(position_logits / temperature)
+            ece = expected_calibration_error(
+                probs,
+                position_labels,
+                num_bins=num_bins,
+            )
+            if ece < best_ece:
+                best_ece = ece
+                best_temperature = float(temperature)
+        temperatures.append(best_temperature)
+        ece_after.append(best_ece)
+
+        calibrated_step = torch.sigmoid(logits[:, position] / best_temperature)
+        raw_step = torch.sigmoid(logits[:, position])
+        calibrated_cumprod = torch.where(
+            position_valid,
+            calibrated_cumprod * calibrated_step,
+            calibrated_cumprod,
+        )
+        raw_cumprod = torch.where(
+            position_valid,
+            raw_cumprod * raw_step,
+            raw_cumprod,
+        )
+        print(
+            f"position {position}: n={num_valid} T={best_temperature:.4f} "
+            f"cumulative ECE {ece_before[-1]:.4f} -> {best_ece:.4f}",
+            flush=True,
+        )
+    return temperatures, ece_before, ece_after
+
+
+def main() -> None:
+    args = parse_args()
+    logits, labels, valid = load_records(args.records)
+
+    grid = torch.logspace(
+        math.log10(args.grid_min),
+        math.log10(args.grid_max),
+        steps=int(args.grid_size),
+        dtype=torch.float64,
+    )
+    # Always include the identity temperature so calibration can no-op.
+    grid = torch.unique(torch.cat([grid, torch.ones(1, dtype=torch.float64)]))
+
+    temperatures, ece_before, ece_after = fit_sequential_temperatures(
+        logits=logits,
+        labels=labels,
+        valid=valid,
+        grid=grid,
+        num_bins=int(args.num_bins),
+    )
+
+    payload = {
+        "temperatures": temperatures,
+        "block_size": logits.shape[1],
+        "num_bins": int(args.num_bins),
+        "grid": {
+            "min": float(args.grid_min),
+            "max": float(args.grid_max),
+            "size": int(args.grid_size),
+        },
+        "num_records": logits.shape[0],
+        "sources": [str(path) for path in args.records],
+        "cumulative_ece_before": ece_before,
+        "cumulative_ece_after": ece_after,
+    }
+    output_path = Path(args.output)
+    output_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
+    with output_path.open("w", encoding="utf-8") as handle:
+        json.dump(payload, handle, ensure_ascii=False, indent=2)
+    print(f"Wrote calibration to {output_path}", flush=True)
+
+
+if __name__ == "__main__":
+    main()

title: test(stream): cover chunk-split and end-of-stream behavior of output parsing
body:
Refs #28.

## Motivation

The stream parser is an incremental state machine: `OutputParser::feed`
retains partial marker matches across chunks, while JSON-mode spacing and
stop-chunk usage accounting are documented as chunk-dependent. Recent
history shows the split dimension and the end-of-stream path are
under-covered: #10 was closed because 0.2.0 documents the
one-space-per-chunk JSON spacing, #14 argues that documented behavior is
inconsistent with every other fixed-output action's `last_pop_action`
dedupe, and #16 fixes end-of-stream loss of text ending in U+FFFD. This PR
pins the current contract systematically, per scenario, so the class is
covered regardless of how #14 lands.

## What this adds

A `#[cfg(test)]` module `stream/split_coverage_tests.rs` (six tests) that
runs a corpus of model-output transcripts through `StreamProcessor` with a
recording `ChunkGenerator` (mirroring the processor's own `Passthrough`
test generator), at every two-way character-boundary split and at a seeded
sample of k-way splits, compared against the single-chunk run or, for JSON
mode, against the analytically computed per-chunk spacing:

- Chunk-transparent scenarios (plain content, thinking mode, DSML tool
  calls with empty and non-ASCII values): normalized `OutputChunk`
  sequences are identical across splits, and completion usage equals the
  transcript's conserved token count. Empty chunks padded around a split
  change nothing.
- JSON mode (fenced and bare): the documented one-space-per-chunk spacing
  is asserted as computed from the split, so adopting #14's per-run spacing
  is a one-line flip of the oracle.
- Stop sequences: emitted text is identical across splits; usage is
  excluded from the comparison because the stop-containing chunk is counted
  whole by contract.
- Token-id splits: a transcript encoded with the bundled V4.1 tokenizer is
  split at every token boundary, covering multi-byte characters split
  across token chunks.
- End of stream: text ending in U+FFFD stays buffered and is dropped
  without text or usage, pinning the behavior `StreamDecoder` documents;
  the expectation carries a flip note for #16.
- A guard that the default special-token spellings the corpus relies on
  (`</think>`, `｜DSML｜`) are unchanged.

Test-only; no behavior change, no new dependencies (split sampling uses a
small seeded xorshift).

## Validation

- `cargo test -p deepseek-recipe`: 56 passed (50 existing + 6 new) on the
  pinned 1.97.1 toolchain.
- `cargo clippy -p deepseek-recipe --all-targets`: no warnings.
- `cargo fmt -p deepseek-recipe -- --check`: clean.
- Sensitivity: flipping the U+FFFD expectation to the post-#16 behavior
  fails on current main, as does replacing the JSON oracle with per-run
  spacing — the harness observes both pinned behaviors.

title: test(stream): systematic chunk-split and end-of-stream coverage for output parsing
body:
### Summary

The stream output parser (`deepseek-recipe/src/stream/output_parser.rs`,
`processor.rs`, `decoder.rs`) is an incremental state machine over backend
chunks. Some of its behavior is chunk-transparent by design — `feed` retains
partial marker matches across chunks, and `ChunkKind` ties special-token
recognition to token boundaries — while other behavior is explicitly
chunk-dependent by contract: JSON-mode spacing is documented as "one space
for each source chunk it spans" and pinned by a processor test, and
completion usage is documented to count the whole chunk containing a matched
stop sequence.

The split dimension is only covered by hand-written cases today, and the
recent history of this layer suggests that is not enough:

- #10 proposed making JSON-mode output independent of chunking and was
  closed unmerged: its author noted v0.2.0 explicitly defines and tests the
  one-space-per-source-chunk behavior, so the PR changed a contract rather
  than fixed a regression.
- #14 (open) now argues that documented behavior is itself wrong: every
  other fixed-output action dedupes consecutive pops through
  `last_pop_action`, only `ToSpace` does not.
- #16 (open) fixes an end-of-stream robustness bug: text legitimately ending
  in U+FFFD stays buffered in `StreamDecoder` forever because `finish()`
  never flushes the decoder, losing it from both content and usage. This one
  is chunking-independent — it fails even with a single chunk.

Whichever way #14 lands, the durable need is the same: systematic coverage
that pins, per scenario, which outputs must be identical across chunk splits
and which are contractually per-chunk — plus end-of-stream robustness.

### Proposal

Stage 1 — an in-crate `#[cfg(test)]` harness (no new dependencies) beside
`output_parser.rs`:

- A corpus of model-output transcripts: thinking on/off, DSML tool calls
  (empty string argument, unicode), JSON mode with fences, a stop sequence
  at several offsets, empty chunks interleaved, and text ending in U+FFFD
  through a stub `StreamTokenizer`.
- For each transcript, run every two-way split at char boundaries and a
  seeded-random sample of k-way splits, asserting:
  - **Chunk-transparent scenarios** (marker/DSML/stop-sequence recognition,
    reasoning and content staging): normalized `OutputChunk` sequences are
    identical across splits.
  - **JSON mode**: pin the currently documented contract (n chunks over a
    replaced run produce n spaces), with the assertion structured so the
    invariance flip is a one-line change if #14 is accepted.
  - **Usage**: without stop sequences, completion usage is identical across
    splits; with stop sequences, only emitted text is compared, since the
    stop-containing chunk is counted whole by contract.
  - **End of stream**: no buffered text or token ids are silently dropped
    (the #16 case; on current main this documents the drop until #16 lands),
    and no input sequence panics.

Stage 2 (optional follow-up) — a `fuzz/` cargo-fuzz target driving the
public `StreamProcessor` with arbitrary `InferenceChunk` sequences, with a
bounded `-runs=N` CI smoke. This needs nightly for `cargo fuzz`, so it can
ride on the CI work in #9 rather than block stage 1.

I maintain the equivalent parser fuzz smoke in agentscope-go (Go), where CI
runs fuzzers that consume untrusted and model-generated data with fixed
execution-count budgets; happy to contribute stage 1 as a PR if the
direction sounds right.

### Notes

- No behavior change is proposed; stage 1 is test-only.
- Stage 1 adds no dev-dependencies: split sampling uses a small seeded RNG.

title: Fix JSON stream output across chunk boundaries
body:
## Summary

- make JSON-mode response text independent of how inference text is split into source chunks
- ignore empty text chunks in the parser while still counting their backend token usage
- add regression coverage for every UTF-8 character boundary, one-character chunks, and empty chunks

## Problem

Outside a detected JSON value, the state machine replaces unmatched text with whitespace so the result remains valid JSON. `StashedChunks` currently emits one space for every backing inference chunk, however. The same model text therefore produces different response content when a backend changes only its chunk boundaries.

On unmodified `8cadfede7063c896b944e7bae05daa3549ae97ea`, the new test fails when the JSON prefix is split after its first character: the split stream produces two leading spaces while the single-chunk stream produces one. An empty text chunk can add another space for the same reason.

The fix emits whitespace once per contiguous `ToSpace` region and keeps empty text out of the parser. Completion-token accounting remains unchanged.

## Testing

Using the repository-pinned Rust 1.97.1 toolchain:

```text
cargo test -p deepseek-recipe --locked
# 2 integration tests passed; doc-tests passed

cargo clippy -p deepseek-recipe --all-targets --locked -- -D warnings
cargo fmt --all -- --check
git diff --check origin/main...HEAD
```

The chunk-invariance test compares a single inference chunk against every valid UTF-8 split point and a stream with one chunk per character. The empty-chunk test also verifies that five completion tokens are retained while response content stays exactly ` {"ok":true} `.

## Scope

This changes only streamed output normalization in JSON mode. It does not change JSON detection, stop-sequence matching, tool-call parsing, protocol schemas, or inference behavior.

title: fix(stream): make JSON-mode ToSpace output independent of backend chunking
body:
## Motivation

In JSON output mode (`parse_json_output`), matched/surrounding text is replaced with spaces via `OutputAction::ToSpace`. Every other fixed-output action (`Label`, `ToolCallBegin`, `ToolNameEnd`, `LabelToolCallArguments`, `ToolCallArgumentsEnd`) deduplicates consecutive pops through `last_pop_action` — exactly because an action spanning chunk boundaries is popped once per whole chunk plus a partial. `ToSpace` had no dedupe, so **one replaced run emitted one space per chunk**: the same model output produced different `content` depending on how the backend split the text (n chunks → up to n spaces), contradicting the documented contract in `state_machine.rs` ("Recognize JSON fences … and replace surrounding text with spaces").

Example: `aaaaabbbb```json\n{}` —
- one `Text` chunk → actions `[ToSpace(9), Skip(8)]` → **one** space;
- two `Text` chunks (`aaaaa` + `bbbb…`) → whole-chunk pop + partial pop → **two** spaces.

## Changes

Consecutive `ToSpace` pops now emit exactly one space per replaced run, using the same `last_pop_action` guard as the other fixed-output actions. No protocol/API change.

## Testing

- New unit test `tospace_output_is_chunk_boundary_independent` feeds the same JSON-mode text whole vs split and asserts identical output. Verified red/green: **fails on the previous implementation** (`left: "  {}" / right: " {}"`), passes with the fix.
- `cargo test -p deepseek-recipe --locked`: pass.

  <details><summary>Proof</summary>

  ```
  running 1 test
  test stream::processor::tospace_tests::tospace_output_is_chunk_boundary_independent ... ok
  test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
  ```

  </details>

title: fix: preserve spaces in DSML tool parameter names
body:
I changed the DSML parameter-name transition to end at the closing quote rather than the next space. Names such as `shipping address` now produce valid JSON keys without losing leading or trailing spaces.

Validation:
- The new regression fails on the original parser and passes with the fix for V4 and V4.1, including every UTF-8-safe two-chunk split and character-sized chunks.
- The protocol-focused Rust suite passes: 6 tests across 8 suites.
- The real decoder HTTP service now returns the expected arguments in Chat Completions, Responses, and Messages formats. The original service returned malformed JSON or an empty argument object.
- Formatting, Clippy with warnings denied, and documentation builds pass for the affected protocol packages.

I did not build the OpenCV-dependent image/Python components.

I used AI assistance for the implementation and regression coverage. The checks above were run through that workflow.

title: fix(stream): flush still-buffered token ids at end of stream
body:
## Motivation

`StreamDecoder::decode` returns `None` whenever the decoded text ends with U+FFFD, assuming a multi-byte character is still split across tokens and the next token will complete it. That heuristic cannot distinguish decoded text that **legitimately** ends with U+FFFD (mojibake bytes decode to a real replacement character — the V4.1 tokenizer has a replacement-character token, so any mojibake output hits this). In that case the ids are never cleared, and since the processor only calls `state_machine.finish()` at end of stream — never flushing the decoder — the buffered text is lost from **both** content and completion usage.

Example: backend streams `Token("a")`, `Token("\u{FFFD}")`, then `Finish{Stop}`. First token emits "a"; the second decodes to `"a\u{FFFD}"` → `ends_with(REPLACEMENT_CHARACTER)` → buffered forever. Final response `content` is `"a"` and `completion_tokens` is 1 instead of 2.

## Changes

- `StreamDecoder::finish()`: flush whatever remains at end of stream — a genuinely truncated sequence yields its replacement character, a legitimate one is emitted instead of dropped.
- The processor feeds the flushed text through the state machine before finishing it, so stop sequences still match in the flushed tail and usage is counted.

## Testing

- New unit test drives `Token` chunks (`a`, U+FFFD) into a `Finish` with a scripted decoder and asserts `content == "a\u{FFFD}"` and `completion_tokens == 2`. Red/green verified: **fails on the previous implementation** (`left: "a" / right: "a\u{FFFD}"`), passes with the fix.
- `cargo test -p deepseek-recipe --locked`: pass.

  <details><summary>Proof</summary>

  ```
  test stream::processor::decoder_flush_tests::trailing_replacement_character_is_flushed_at_end_of_stream ... ok
  test result: ok. 1 passed; 0 failed
  ```

  </details>

title: perf(cake_deepgemm_mega_mhc): two-lane Sinkhorn normalization chain on the 40- and 27-split mHC programs (SM100a, SM103a)
body:
This PR speeds up the Cake fused manifold hyper-connection (mHC) kernel (`flashinfer.experimental.deepgemm_mega_mhc`, public API `flashinfer.mega_mhc.prepare_mega_mhc`). It is one persistent kernel that fuses the mHC residual-stream mixing of DeepSeek V4.1 Flash at hidden size 5120. That covers the FP8-normalized comb/post/pre mixing GEMV work, a 4 x 4 Sinkhorn normalization (20 iterations) of the mixing matrix, the residual update, and the BF16 / FP8 outputs with their scale factors. The exported family has 4 routes: col and extra layouts, each in plain and shifted form. The token range is split into 4 split-count classes chosen at generation time: 40 splits for T <= 192, 27 for 193 <= T <= 320, 20 for 321 <= T <= 448 and 16 for T >= 449. That gives one compiled program per route and split class, and one source per program serves both architectures. This PR delivers the 40- and 27-split programs (T <= 320). In these programs the Mix role now runs the 4 x 4 Sinkhorn chain on two lanes, with in-register row sums and one xor-1 shuffle per iteration. Before, it ran on 16 lanes with shuffle-reduced row and column sums. Each element goes through the same operations on the same values in the same order, so outputs are bit-identical. Inputs, outputs, quantization formats, scale layouts and the `prepare_mega_mhc` signature are unchanged. The baseline is the previous Cake version of this family on FlashInfer main. Most of the gain is at T = 200, the 27-split class, at 1.022-1.050x on both architectures. The GB300 T = 64/65 rows gain 1.005-1.026x. On B200 the T = 64/65 rows are mixed (0.987-1.015x). The T = 1 rows show no consistent gain (0.966-1.024x), and the lowest is GB300 extra plain at 0.966x. So the two-lane chain mainly helps the 27-split programs.

Timings are CUPTI kernel-time medians of the whole call, not CUDA events. Each row is one launch, with L2 flushed before every launch. Each cell is the median of 12 readings per architecture. On B200 these came from eight distinct GPUs over two allocations of the same node class. On GB300 they came from four distinct GPUs of one node, each read three times. All shapes use hidden size 5120 with the listed token count T, and route = layout (col / extra) x form (plain / shifted). Speedup = previous / this PR. Rows with T <= 320 run the changed program. Rows with T >= 1025 run byte-identical programs on both sides, measured in separate passes, so their ratios show measurement spread: 0.999-1.003x on B200 and 1.003-1.013x on GB300.

title: [cake deslop] mega_gate/mhc/moe_v3 (2): fold mHC binding/split-40 clones, drop caller-less MoE routes, retire 6 exact-shape gate programs
body:
**Background.** The DeepGEMM-signature mega families are Cake-generated and JIT-compiled lazily per selected program and per arch (sm_100a/sm_103a). None of them is in `flashinfer/aot.py`. The families are `flashinfer.mega_gate` (`csrc/experimental/deepgemm_mega_gate`, 15 programs), `flashinfer.mega_mhc` (`csrc/experimental/deepgemm_mega_mhc`, 10 programs / 16 routes) and `flashinfer.mega_moe_v3` (`csrc/experimental/mega_moe_v3`, 13 programs / 10 routes in `catalog.json`). The unit also owns the hand-written `csrc/mhc` (#3285, AOT and JIT via `gen_mhc_module`), which is not Cake bloat. At 3184bbea the unit has 103 files and about 78.5K lines. The first round already landed: #5833 (mega_gate runtime token count, 11 per-M kernels collapsed) was closed by #5961 (+6103/−25606). #5834 (24 near-identical mHC kernels → one parametrized kernel) was closed by #5955 (+4923/−59387). #5842/#5843 (mega_moe_v3 + source_mega_moe) were closed by #5904 (+2353/−42679). After that round, #6029 added the FP4 1024/4096-token pipeline programs (2 more exact-shape routes) and #6031 retired source_mega_moe. #6034 merged the per-arch catalog but kept the t16/t128 per-arch pairs. #6129 (+2652/−419) renamed all mega_gate programs and added `99c1c61a` and `8b22b176` (13 → 15 programs, +1,939 `.cu` lines). The mHC sources have not changed since #5955. Every `.cu` file is in a loader table. All equivalence claims below are source-level, made after normalising hashes and arch names. Each mechanical step must be confirmed with a per-(program, defines, arch) `cuobjdump -sass` diff.

**Findings**
- **mHC bindings: 10 identical copies.** All 10 `deepgemm_mega_mhc/generated/cake_mega_mhc_*_binding.cu` files are 539 lines. Once the 20-hex program hash and the 16-hex host-shim namespace are neutralised, they are identical; any two differ in 8 line positions. `load_program` (`mega_mhc.py:404-434`) already passes `-D` defines. No code in `flashinfer/` or `tests/` reads the `kernel_symbol` field in `PROGRAMS`. Removable: 4,851 lines.
- **mHC split-40 clones.** The split-40 kernels `45d5adeb`, `f9701d86`, `557f4193` and `f87d829e` (5,173 lines) differ from their split-20/27 twins `35a28241`, `f7faf2e5`, `7d69b178` and `078e8965` by 4/4/16/16 lines. The differences are `#pragma unroll 1` vs `#pragma unroll`, plus a 14-line `if (num_tokens < 64)` block in the shifted pair. `NUM_SPLITS` is already a per-route compile-line define (`mega_mhc.py:146-275`), and the kernels `#error` without it (lines 56-63). The remaining variants differ by 15 lines (shared_sf on/off), 64/88 lines (shifted split-16 vs split-20/27) and 733 lines (shifted vs non-shifted, a real variant).
- **mega_gate exact-shape programs.** `prepare_mega_gate` only accepts K=5120, E=384, top-k 6 on (10,0)/(10,3). Six of the 15 programs are exact-shape: `f78ed5c2`, `8b22b176`, `c01e013d`, `a8833c33`, `ab8ab2e2`, `3ca2bfdf` (`TEMPLATES[10..15]`, `static_tokens` {1,4,16,16,128,512}). `select_template` (`mega_gate.py:1130-1142`) returns them only when `_tile_geometry`, `static_route` and `static_workers` all match. Otherwise it returns the runtime twin with identical `_schedule_axes`: `8be2bbbc`, `99c1c61a`, `aeda81f0` (twin of two programs), `3561d17e` and `882c4420`. Each kernel differs from its twin by 47–110 lines of constant folding (`tile < 1; tile += 6`, literal idesc, pruned `route_flags & 1`); the bindings are identical. These programs are selected for:
  - M=1;
  - M=2..4 on sm_100a only (`SMALL_M_CLUSTER_SPLIT16_ARCHES`, line 857);
  - M=5..16 (sm_100a) / 2..16 (sm_103a) physical, and the same window logical-only;
  - M=113..128 and M=497..512.

  They are the README's production rows (M=1, 3, 16, 128, 512) and `test_routing_values_stream_and_replay` runs them on GPU. Removing them (5,687 lines) is therefore a benchmark-gated twin replacement, not a dead-code delete. `99c1c61a` and `8b22b176` are never selected or compiled on sm_103a.
- **mega_gate runtime programs split by split-K.** `443ee721` already serves TEMPLATES 6 and 7 through `template <int kNumSplitK>`. Other block-16/176 programs differ from each other by 106–188 lines. After hash normalisation the 15 bindings reduce to 7 distinct texts. Folding the 9 runtime programs would mean regenerating them; that saves roughly 2–3K lines (low confidence, not counted).
- **mega_moe_v3 caller-less surfaces.** `prepare_grouped_fused` and `prepare_grouped_l1` appear only in:
  - `runtime.py` and `flashinfer/mega_moe_v3.py`;
  - `catalog.json` and the generated `.cu` files;
  - a structural special case at `test_mega_moe_v3_catalog.py:35`.

  Every `bind_prepared` caller (`test_generated_mega_moe.py`, `examples/experimental/mega_moe_inputs.py:154-173`) uses pipeline or grouped_l2. grouped_l1 is a toy shape (E=4 × 256 rows, N=256, K=512, grid 16). grouped_fused carries `benchmark: true`, but the used grouped_l2 route carries it too. Both surfaces date from #5523, and #5904 listed them as "deliberately unchanged". They are public experimental exports, so the source tree cannot rule out an external caller. Removable: 4,420 lines (4,047 `.cu`, 326 catalog; the rest runtime/wrapper/test/docs).
- **mega_moe_v3 per-arch pairs.** The fp4 t16 and t128 pipeline programs ship as sm100a/sm103a pairs: t16 is 3,002/3,037 lines and t128 is 2,996/3,034 lines. Their 718-line bindings are identical after normalisation. The kernel pairs differ by 83/72 lines in three ways:
  - `#define NUM_CTAS 148` vs `152`;
  - hoisted `selected_weight_map` pointer selection;
  - asm-volatile operand wrappers around the same `tcgen05_cp` / `tcgen05_mma_mxf8_bs_cta2` / `tma_2d_gmem2smem_cta2` calls.

  The other 7 pipeline programs are already arch-neutral via `#ifndef NUM_CTAS` + `-DNUM_CTAS`. The pairs hold 7,507 redundant lines. Whether the two forms produce the same SASS is unverified (medium confidence).
- **Exact shapes and exact SM counts.** mega_moe_v3 `runtime.key()` builds an exact JSON key. `_route` raises on a miss, and `_route_arch` raises unless the device has exactly 148 (sm_100a) or 152 (sm_103a) SMs. The 7 pipeline routes are fp4 T ∈ {1, 16, 128, 512, 1024, 4096} and fp8 T=16, all at (384, 6, 5120, 2304, clamp 10.0). T=128 and T=512 have no test. `preparation.py:186-199` hard-codes `persistent_grid in (148,152)`. mHC `num_launch_sms` (`mega_mhc.py:329-361`) trims the grid only at benchmark points (148/152 SMs, hidden 5120, T ∈ {1, 64, 65}), and no test asserts its value.
- **Manifest and host-code bloat.**
  - `catalog.json` (3,113 lines) repeats one 58-entry `arg_plan` across 9 pipeline programs: 1,872 redundant lines. `cake_catalog.py` has no shared-key support.
  - `mega_gate.py` `PROGRAMS` (lines 28-584) repeats one 27-entry `arg_plan` 15×. A module-level `ARG_PLAN`, which `mega_mhc.py` already uses, would save ~370 lines.
  - The unit has 3 copies of `DEEPGEMM_NOTICE.txt` (59 lines); 80 sources cite it by name. It also has two `host_common.cuh` files (55/39 lines) that both define `CakeSetMaxDynamicSmem`.
  - In `preparation.py`, the constants `pr432_optimizations = True` and `capture_l1 = False` (131-132) leave ~30 lines of else-branches (215-256) that no bound plan reaches (medium confidence).
- **Per-call host work.** The generated `run()` re-validates operands and re-encodes TMA descriptors on every launch. mega_gate runs ~60 checks over 15 tensors plus 2 `cuTensorMapEncodeTiled` calls; mHC runs 22 tensor checks plus 8 encodes; pipeline t1 runs 108 `TVM_FFI_CHECK*` plus 9 tensor maps. Only the grouped bindings export `run_prepare`. At prepare time, `_mega_dispatch_reference` calls `.item()` in a loop T×TK times. The host-time cost has not been measured.
- **Broken example drivers.** `examples/experimental/mega_moe.py` and `bench_mega_moe.py` (90 lines) default `--family` to `source`, which #6031 retired. They call `make_model(args.family, args.precision, args.tokens)`, but #6031 changed the signature to `make_model(precision, num_tokens=16, ...)`. Neither script runs, and nothing imports them. The held-out list in `deepgemm_mega_gate/README.md:50-52` is missing the count 400 that `test_mega_gate_generated.py:32` uses.
- **csrc/mhc.** This code is hand-written and lean. All public template instantiations are reachable; only ~20 lines of `launch_vec_plan` constexpr arms are never instantiated. `flashinfer/mhc.py` forces inputs contiguous with 15 `.contiguous()` calls, and the mega plans reject non-contiguous inputs (low priority). No step proposed.
- **Tests that pin removals (update in the same PR).**
  - `test_mega_gate_generated.py::test_every_token_count_selects_an_exported_template` has a `static_tokens` dict at lines 101-110.
  - `test_mega_moe_v3_catalog.py::test_every_route_resolves_its_programs_grid_and_sm_count` special-cases grouped_l1.
  - `::test_programs_sources_symbols_and_compile_line_definitions` asserts `#define NUM_CTAS <sms>`, and that each binding is named `<name>_binding.cu` and contains `kernel_<name>(`.
  - `::test_load_program_supplies_the_route_sm_count_as_num_ctas` checks the spec names.
  - `test_deepgemm_common.py::test_every_family_catalog_in_the_tree_loads` requires per-program `sources` and `compile_flags`.
  - `test_mega_mhc_generated.py` pins no program hash.
  - `deepgemm_mega_gate/README.md` and `docs/experimental/generated_mega_moe.md` describe the exact-shape programs, the grouped fused route and the per-arch pairs.

**Proposed steps**
- [ ] Replace the 10 mHC bindings with one shared binding (9 files, −4,851). Use a uniform kernel symbol or `-DKERNEL_SYMBOL` on the compile line, repoint each `PROGRAMS` entry in `mega_mhc.py`, and drop the `kernel_symbol` field. Kernel TUs stay unchanged, so `cuobjdump -sass` must be byte-identical for each of the 10 programs × {sm_100a, sm_103a} × its `NUM_SPLITS`. Then run `test_mega_mhc_generated.py` on B200 and B300/GB300.
- [ ] Fold the 4 split-40 mHC kernels into their split-20/27 twins (4 files, −5,173). Wrap the unroll pragmas (lines 856/964 or 917) and the 14-line `if (num_tokens < 64)` block in `#if NUM_SPLITS == 40`. Repoint the 4 `num_splits=40` ROUTES and extend the twins' `num_splits` lists. Confirm per-(program, NUM_SPLITS, arch) SASS identity; T=1/64/65 exercise split 40 on 148/152 SMs.
- [ ] Delete the mega_moe_v3 grouped_fused/grouped_l1 surfaces (−4,420):
  - the 4 `deepgemm_mega_moe_v3_grouped_{fused,l1}_{kernel,binding}.cu` files;
  - the 2 programs and 2 routes in `catalog.json`;
  - the `runtime.key()` grouped_l1 branch, the `V3Plan` docstring paragraph, and `prepare_grouped_fused`/`prepare_grouped_l1` with their re-exports in `flashinfer/mega_moe_v3.py`;
  - the special case at `test_mega_moe_v3_catalog.py:35-37` and `docs/experimental/generated_mega_moe.md:31-32`.

  Before merging, search the org repos for callers and ask for downstream objections; #5904 kept these public exports deliberately. Run `test_generated_mega_moe.py`, `test_mega_moe_v3_catalog.py` and `test_deepgemm_common.py` on a 148-SM B200 and, if one is available, a 152-SM sm_103a device.
- [ ] Deduplicate manifests and host code (−2,331):

  - add a module-level `ARG_PLAN` in `mega_gate.py` (−370);
  - keep a single `DEEPGEMM_NOTICE.txt` under `csrc/experimental/`, with the same name (−59);
  - remove the `capture_l1`/non-`source_schedule`/`reset_storage is None` branches in `preparation.py` (−30; confirm no bound plan reaches them);

- [ ] Fix or delete `examples/experimental/mega_moe.py` and `bench_mega_moe.py` (−90 if deleted). To fix them, drop the retired `source` family and call `make_model(args.precision, args.tokens)`; if kept, run `--tokens 16` on a 148-SM B200. Add 400 to the README held-out list.
- [ ] Retire the 6 exact-shape mega_gate programs so that `select_template` always returns the runtime twin (12 `.cu` files + `PROGRAMS`/`TEMPLATES[10..15]`, −5,687). Gate the change on a benchmark: run twin vs static at M ∈ {1, 2, 3, 4, 8, 16, 128, 512}, with and without the physical map, on B200 and B300. Keep only rows that regress beyond noise and record the numbers in the PR. Relax the pinned test (lines 101-110) and the README paragraph. For correctness, run `EXPORTED_ROWS` and `HELD_OUT` on B200 and sm_103a.
- [ ] Merge the t16/t128 sm100a/sm103a pairs into arch-neutral programs with `#ifndef NUM_CTAS` + `-DNUM_CTAS` (−7,507, not counted). This needs regeneration or a hand-merge. Check the merged source with a cuobjdump SASS diff against each current per-arch build, then run the T=16 fp4 test and a new T=128 run. Benchmark both arches, because the pairs differ in codegen form. Update `test_mega_moe_v3_catalog.py` (41-44, 66-70), catalog routes 2751-2754/2797-2800 and the docs.

Then `run()` no longer re-validates 15–33 tensors or re-encodes 2/8/9 TMA descriptors per call. Vectorize `_mega_dispatch_reference` with `torch.bincount`. Measure `plan.run()` host time before and after on B200. Outputs must match bit-exactly, and the `check_single_kernel_graph` tests must pass.

title: feat(mhc): add experimental mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm
body:
## 📌 Description This PR adds **`flashinfer.mhc.mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm`** as an **experimental API**. The op is the pre-finalize step of a manifold-constrained hyper-connection (mHC) boundary with `HC = 4` residual streams. It also fuses the next sublayer's RMSNorm into its output. On SM100 / SM103, decode batches run a new thread-block-cluster kernel. Every other call runs a composable fp32 PyTorch implementation of the same contract, so the API always returns a result. ### Model and use case - **Model:** the op was written for decode of [GLM-5.3-Flash](https://huggingface.co/RedHatAI/GLM-5.3-Flash-NVFP4) (hidden size 4096, `hc_mult = 4`, 45 layers) on GB300. - **Call count:** every attention and every MoE sublayer is wrapped by an mHC boundary, so the op runs **90 times per decode step**. - **Current vLLM path:** for batches of up to 32 tokens, vLLM runs each boundary as two kernels: 1. `mhc_fused` mixes the sublayer output back into the 4 residual streams and computes split-K partials of the 24 mix logits. 2. A **pre-finalize** kernel, written in TileLang. It runs one 96-thread CTA per token, so a decode token's whole pre-finalize runs on a single SM. - **This PR** implements step 2. ```mermaid flowchart LR B["sublayer output
(attention or MoE)"] --> F["mhc_fused
mix into the 4 residual streams
+ split-K partials of the 24 mix logits"] F -->|"gemm_out_mul [NS, T, 24] fp32
gemm_out_sqrsum [NS, T] fp32
residual [T, 4, 4096] bf16"| P["mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm
(this PR)"] P -->|"layer_input [T, 4096] bf16
(already RMSNorm'd)"| N["next sublayer
(attention or MoE)"] P -->|"post_mix [T, 4]
comb_mix [T, 4, 4]"| F2["next boundary's
mhc_fused"] N --> F2 ``` ### What is fused ```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph BEFORE["Before: stable FlashInfer APIs, two kernels"] direction LR A1["split-K partials
+ residual"] --> K1["mhc_pre_big_fuse
reduce logits → sigmoids
→ Sinkhorn → weighted sum"] K1 -->|"un-normalized layer_input
bf16, round trip through HBM"| K2["rmsnorm"] K2 --> O1["layer_input"] K1 --> M1["post_mix, comb_mix"] end subgraph AFTER["After: this PR, one kernel"] direction LR A2["split-K partials
+ residual + norm_weight"] --> K3["mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm
reduce logits → sigmoids → Sinkhorn
→ weighted sum → RMSNorm"] K3 --> O2["layer_input"] K3 --> M2["post_mix, comb_mix"] end BEFORE ~~~ AFTER ``` | step | computes | |---|---| | 1. reduce partials | `mixes = Σ_s gemm_out_mul[s] · rsqrt(Σ_s gemm_out_sqrsum[s] / (4·H) + rms_eps)` | | 2. pre | `pre = sigmoid(mixes[0:4]·hc_scale[0] + hc_base[0:4]) + hc_pre_eps` | | 3. post_mix | `post_mix = sigmoid(mixes[4:8]·hc_scale[1] + hc_base[4:8]) · hc_post_mult_value` | | 4. comb_mix | 20-iteration Sinkhorn of `softmax(mixes[8:24] as 4×4) + hc_sinkhorn_eps` | | 5. weighted sum | `ol = Σ_j pre[j] · residual[:, j, :]` (fp32) | | **6. RMSNorm (newly fused)** | `layer_input = bf16(bf16(ol) · rsqrt(mean(ol²) + norm_eps) · norm_weight)` | - Fusing the RMSNorm removes one launch and the `[T, 4096]` bf16 round trip through HBM (8 KB written and read back per token). The RMS statistic is taken on the fp32 sum `ol` rather than on its bf16 copy. - vLLM's current TileLang kernel already fuses the same six steps, but on one CTA per token. The speedups under Performance are measured against that kernel, so they come from the cluster design below, not from removing a launch. - Per token the op reads 32 KB of residual and writes 8 KB. It is latency-bound, not bandwidth-bound: on one CTA, the 20-iteration Sinkhorn chain, the 4096-wide weighted sum and the RMSNorm reduction run one after another. ### Kernel design (`mhc_pre_cluster_kernel`) ```mermaid flowchart LR subgraph OLD["one CTA per token (current)"] direction TB T0["1 CTA, 96 threads, 1 SM"] --> T1["logits → sigmoids → softmax → 20× Sinkhorn"] T1 --> T2["weighted sum over 4096 channels"] T2 --> T3["RMSNorm → store"] end subgraph NEW["thread-block cluster per token (this PR)"] direction TB C0["4-CTA cluster per token
(2-CTA when T > 24)"] C0 --> R["warps 1-2 of every CTA: 1024 channels each
weighted sum + Σ ol² partial"] R --> X["all-gather of Σ ol² over DSMEM
(st.async + mbarrier)"] X --> Y["each CTA normalizes and stores its slice"] C0 --> S["warp 0 of rank 1: softmax +
division-free Sinkhorn → comb_mix"] C0 --> Q["warp 0 of the post rank:
post sigmoid → post_mix"] end ``` **Parallel layout** - The weighted sum and the RMSNorm are split across the cluster. - The only cross-CTA step is a single all-gather of the RMSNorm partial sums over distributed shared memory. - The Sinkhorn and the post sigmoid run on spare warps, concurrently with the weighted sum. - Every warp issues its global loads first, so a token costs one DRAM round trip. **Division-free Sinkhorn** - The matrix is kept in diagonal-scaling form `c = r · K · s / G`. - Cofactor products replace the per-step divisions. - The common denominator is renormalised by exact powers of two. - A single Newton-refined reciprocal produces the final `1/G`. - An exact power-of-two rebalance of `r` and `s` after every column half-step keeps both within `(2^-64, 2^50)` for every finite input. The rebalance changes no rounding. **Numerics** - The module is built without `-use_fast_math`. - `expf` is libdevice, and the post sigmoid uses IEEE division. - The pre sigmoids and `1/G` use Newton-refined reciprocals. - `rsqrt.approx` is applied only to arguments `>= 1e-5`. - fp32 add, mul and fma never flush to zero. **Launch** - One `cudaLaunchKernelEx`, with the cluster shape compiled in (`__cluster_dims__`). - Optional PDL (`enable_pdl=True`): the kernel reads no input before `griddepcontrol.wait`, and uses plain `ld.global` because `.nc` loads would be hoisted above the wait. - ptxas: 110 registers (4-CTA cluster) / 165–168 registers (2-CTA cluster), 0 spills, 112–128 B static shared memory. ### API surface All three functions are `@flashinfer_experimental_api`; calling any of them is the opt-in, and each warns once. | Function | Purpose | |---|---| | `mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm(...)` | The op. Optional caller-owned outputs and `enable_pdl`. | | `mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm_supported(...)` | Returns True when this exact call runs the cluster kernel. A framework keeps its own path whenever it returns False. | | `mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm_warmup(device)` | Builds and loads the kernel before CUDA-graph capture. The kernel is never built during capture; a capturing call without a loaded module captures the composable path. | **Kernel envelope** - SM100 / SM103. - `H = 4096`, `HC = 4`, `1 <= T <= 32`, `NS ∈ {8, 64}`. - Compiled-in model constants: `rms_eps = norm_eps = 1e-5`, `hc_pre_eps = hc_sinkhorn_eps = 1e-6`, `hc_post_mult_value = 2`, `sinkhorn_repeat = 20`. The support check compares them as fp32. - Dense, 16-byte-aligned tensors. `FLASHINFER_SPECIALIZED_KERNEL_DISABLE=1`, read at call time, forces the composable path. This is the existing switch from `mla_kv_pack`; its `CLAUDE.md` row is updated. **Layout** - Core: thin entry points in `flashinfer/mhc.py` (signature, shared validation, deferred-import handoff). - Everything else lives in `flashinfer/experimental/mhc_pre_big_fuse_with_norm/`: kernel, JIT spec, support check, composable implementation and a README with the user contract. - JIT-only, with nothing in `aot.py`. No trace template yet. ### Performance **Kernel level** (GB300, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.13.0+cu130) - Metric: CUPTI device time, median of 200 iterations after 20 warmup, inside CUDA-graph replay, PDL off. - *Cold*: L2 flushed before every call. *Warm*: 16 back-to-back calls per graph (serving-like). - Baseline: vLLM's TileLang pre-finalize kernel (vLLM nightly of 2026-10-08), measured in the same session on the same GPU. | T | NS | TileLang cold (µs) | **this PR cold (µs)** | speedup | TileLang warm (µs) | **this PR warm (µs)** | speedup | |---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 8 | 5.376 | **2.752** | 1.95× | 5.152 | **2.144** | 2.40× | | 2 | 8 | 4.992 | **2.592** | 1.93× | 4.704 | **2.224** | 2.12× | | 4 | 8 | 5.184 | **2.912** | 1.78× | 4.736 | **2.240** | 2.11× | | 8 | 8 | 5.216 | **2.912** | 1.79× | 5.088 | **2.272** | 2.24× | | 16 | 8 | 5.248 | **3.008** | 1.74× | 5.184 | **2.400** | 2.16× | | 24 | 8 | 5.280 | **3.136** | 1.68× | 5.216 | **2.432** | 2.14× | | 32 | 8 | 5.280 | **3.200** | 1.65× | 5.024 | **2.464** | 2.04× | | 1 | 64 | 6.112 | **2.976** | 2.05× | 5.472 | **2.304** | 2.38× | | 2 | 64 | 5.936 | **3.040** | 1.95× | 5.056 | **2.432** | 2.08× | | 4 | 64 | 5.664 | **3.200** | 1.77× | 5.088 | **2.592** | 1.96× | | 8 | 64 | 6.112 | **3.328** | 1.84× | 5.408 | **2.624** | 2.06× | | 16 | 64 | 6.144 | **3.392** | 1.81× | 5.536 | **2.577** | 2.15× | | 24 | 64 | 6.016 | **3.488** | 1.72× | 5.568 | **2.608** | 2.13× | | 32 | 64 | 6.112 | **3.616** | 1.69× | 5.344 | **2.624** | 2.04× | | **geomean** | | 5.604 | **3.099** | **1.81×** | 5.178 | **2.419** | **2.14×** | **Per decode step** (nsys, c=1, 90 calls per step) | per decode step | before | after | change | |---|---:|---:|---:| | mHC pre-finalize | 0.433 ms | 0.239 ms | **−0.195 ms** | | `mhc_fused` (unchanged) | 0.516 ms | 0.515 ms | −0.001 ms | **End to end** (vLLM) - Setup: GLM-5.3-Flash NVFP4, vLLM nightly of 2026-10-08, TP8 across two 4-GPU GB300 nodes, agentic-coding multi-turn session replay, 1800 s per concurrency point. - Both arms use the same build. vLLM calls this API through a small patch that is not part of this PR. - In the baseline arm, `FLASHINFER_SPECIALIZED_KERNEL_DISABLE=1` makes `_supported()` return False, so vLLM keeps its TileLang kernel. | concurrency | mean ITL before → after | mean ITL | ITL p50 | ITL p99 | TTFT p50 | output tok/s | |---|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:| | 1 | 4.457 → 4.134 ms | **−7.2%** | −5.4% | −7.0% | −6.7% | **+3.2%** | | 8 (2 pairs pooled) | 5.547 → 5.299 ms | **−4.5%** | −5.4% | −7.1% | +9.0%¹ | −0.4% | | 64 | 15.477 → 15.044 ms | **−2.8%** | −3.8% | +6.1% | −6.2% | **+2.1%** | ¹ Prefill runs identical code in both arms; one of the two allocations was slower at prefill. Normalising each run by its allocation's prefill speed gives TTFT p50 +4.0% and mean ITL −5.3% at c=8. The gain shrinks with concurrency because the kernel serves only batches of up to 32 tokens. At higher concurrency, more of each step is prefill or larger batches. ## 🔍 Related Issues ## 🚀 Pull Request Checklist Thank you for contributing to FlashInfer! Before we review your pull request, please make sure the following items are complete. ### ✅ Pre-commit Checks - [ ] I have installed `pre-commit` by running `pip install pre-commit` (or used your preferred method). - [ ] I have installed the hooks with `pre-commit install`. - [ ] I have run the hooks manually with `pre-commit run --all-files` and fixed any reported issues. > If you are unsure about how to set up `pre-commit`, see [the pre-commit documentation](https://pre-commit.com/). ## 🧪 Tests - [ ] Tests have been added or updated as needed. - [ ] All tests are passing (`unittest`, etc.). ## 🔬 Experimental Track - [x] This PR is **experimental**: it adds or changes code under `flashinfer/experimental/` and/or an `@flashinfer_experimental_api`. Tracking issue: # - [ ] The tracking issue names an owner, the reason for the experimental path, and a graduation plan with a target release. - [x] Core changes are limited to a thin entry point (signature, shared validation, feature-gate check, backend selection, handoff). - [x] Tests live in `tests/experimental/` and were validated on the intended hardware; a runnable example is included. - [x] Nothing is registered in `flashinfer/aot.py`, and no experimental backend is reachable from `backend="auto"` without `FLASHINFER_ALLOW_EXPERIMENTAL_AUTO_BACKENDS=1`.
